pillar: Bone Marrow Transplant in India for International Patients

items.q: Am I eligible for a bone marrow transplant in India?
items.a: Eligibility for a bone marrow transplant in India depends on the specific diagnosis — such as acute or chronic leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, severe aplastic anemia, thalassemia major, or sickle cell disease — along with disease stage, donor availability, and overall organ function, and can only be confirmed after a hematology specialist reviews complete medical records. A pre-transplant work-up typically includes blood counts, a bone marrow biopsy, imaging, and organ function tests to assess fitness for the procedure, alongside HLA typing to check for a matching donor. Final eligibility should be discussed with a qualified oncology team, since it depends on cancer type, stage, biomarker profile, prior treatment, and specialist review.

items.q: What types of bone marrow transplant are performed in India?
items.a: Indian transplant centers perform five main types of bone marrow transplant — autologous using the patient's own stem cells, allogeneic from a matched sibling, allogeneic from a haploidentical half-matched family donor, allogeneic from a registry-matched unrelated donor, and cord blood transplant — with the choice depending on donor availability and diagnosis. Autologous transplant is commonly used for multiple myeloma and some relapsed lymphomas, matched sibling and haploidentical transplants are used for acute leukemia and thalassemia, and unrelated donor or cord blood options are considered when no suitable family donor is found. Which type applies to a specific case depends on diagnosis, stage, biomarker profile, and specialist review, and should be confirmed by the treating oncology team.

items.q: How much does a bone marrow transplant cost in India?
items.a: Bone marrow transplant costs in India are estimated to range from about $12,000–$30,000 for an autologous transplant, $25,000–$55,000 for a matched sibling allogeneic transplant, $35,000–$70,000 for a haploidentical transplant, and $40,000–$85,000 or more for a matched unrelated donor transplant, depending on conditioning regimen, hospital, and complications. Pre-transplant evaluation and HLA typing typically add another $500 to $1,500 depending on how many family members are tested, and haploidentical or unrelated-donor transplants tend to cost more than a matched sibling transplant because of additional donor workup. These are estimated ranges only; a precise cost estimate is only possible after your medical reports and transplant type are reviewed by the treating hospital.

items.q: What is the success rate of a bone marrow transplant in India?
items.a: There is no single, universal success rate for bone marrow transplant in India, because outcomes vary widely by diagnosis, disease stage, transplant type — autologous, matched sibling, haploidentical, unrelated donor, or cord blood — donor match quality, age, and overall organ function at the time of transplant. Autologous transplants for conditions like multiple myeloma generally carry a different risk profile than allogeneic transplants, which need close monitoring for graft-versus-host disease and infection during the weeks after stem cell infusion. Individual outcome expectations may be considered only after a qualified oncology team reviews the complete case, and no transplant approach can be guaranteed to cure or control disease in every patient.

items.q: Can I still get a bone marrow transplant in India without a matched sibling donor?
items.a: Yes, a bone marrow transplant may still be possible without a matched sibling donor, since Indian transplant centers can evaluate a haploidentical half-matched family donor, search unrelated donor registries, or consider a cord blood transplant, depending on the patient's diagnosis, urgency, and overall clinical picture. Haploidentical transplants use a half-matched parent or child when no full match exists in the family, unrelated donor transplants rely on registry matching, and cord blood transplant is considered when no matched adult donor can be found. Which alternative donor option, if any, may be considered depends on HLA typing results, diagnosis, and specialist review, and should be confirmed by the treating transplant team.

items.q: What happens during a bone marrow transplant procedure?
items.a: A bone marrow transplant in India generally follows a set sequence — medical evaluation, donor search and HLA matching, stem cell collection, conditioning therapy with chemotherapy or radiation, stem cell infusion, and engraftment — followed by a period of close monitoring and recovery that can last weeks to months. Stem cells are collected from peripheral blood after growth-factor injections or directly from bone marrow under anesthesia, and the collected cells are then infused like a blood transfusion, with engraftment usually beginning within two to four weeks. The exact sequence and timing can vary by transplant type and individual case, and should be discussed in detail with the treating oncology team.

items.q: How long do I need to stay in India for a bone marrow transplant?
items.a: Total stay in India for a bone marrow transplant is generally around 4 to 6 weeks for an autologous transplant and about 8 to 14 weeks or more for an allogeneic transplant, covering pre-transplant evaluation, hospital admission, stem cell infusion, and early post-transplant recovery. Allogeneic and pediatric transplants often require a longer stay because of the additional monitoring needed for engraftment and graft-versus-host disease, and an accompanying family member or donor may also need to plan for an extended stay. Actual duration depends on transplant type, complications, and recovery progress, and should be confirmed with the treating hospital before travel is finalized.

items.q: Which Indian cities offer bone marrow transplant treatment?
items.a: Bone marrow transplant is offered in several major Indian cities, including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bangalore, and Kochi and Vellore, each with established hematology and transplant programs covering both adult and pediatric cases across a range of transplant types. Delhi NCR and Mumbai are major hubs for adult and pediatric transplant with strong infection-control units and high transplant volumes, Chennai and Kochi/Vellore have long-standing pediatric and thalassemia transplant programs, and Hyderabad and Bangalore have growing transplant capacity with strong laboratory and blood bank infrastructure. The right city and center depend on diagnosis, transplant type, and donor availability, and should be selected in consultation with a specialist reviewing the case.

items.q: What are the risks of a bone marrow transplant?
items.a: A bone marrow transplant is a major treatment with real, well-documented risks, including infections, low blood counts, and bleeding, and allogeneic transplants carry an added risk of graft-versus-host disease, a condition that requires careful, ongoing monitoring by the transplant team. Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor immune cells react against the recipient's tissues and can range from mild to serious, which is why allogeneic transplant recipients are monitored closely for weeks to months after stem cell infusion. These risks vary by transplant type, age, and overall health, and should be reviewed individually with the treating oncology team before any decision is made.

items.q: How can international patients get support for a bone marrow transplant in India?
items.a: International patients considering a bone marrow transplant in India can access support with medical visa guidance, travel arrangements for an accompanying family member or donor, language assistance, and planning for the longer stay that allogeneic or pediatric transplant may require. CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or trials, estimate costs, and coordinate travel, visa, and follow-up support alongside the treating oncology team. All treatment decisions, including transplant type and hospital selection, should be made by the treating medical team based on a full review of the case.
